Labor and Birth 
Complications

Preterm Labor and Birth  
 Preterm birth and prematurity describes length of gestation, regardless of 
birth weight < 37 6/7 weeks
 Low birth weight describes only birth weight:
 2500 g or less
 Easier to measure than preterm birth
 Preterm birth is more dangerous
 Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR)
 Inadequate fetal growth
 Spontaneous preterm birth
 An early initiation of the labor process
 Comprises 75% of preterm births

Risk Factors for PTL
 African American race (doubles the risk)
 • Maternal age extremes (<16 years and >40 
years old)
 • Low socioeconomic status
 • Alcohol or other drug use, especially cocaine
 • Poor maternal nutrition
 • Maternal periodontal disease
 • Cigarette smoking
 • Low level of education
 • History of prior preterm birth (triples the risk)
 • Uterine abnormalities, such as fibroids
 • Low pregnancy weight for height
 • Preexisting diabetes or hypertension
 • Multiple pregnancy
 • Premature rupture of membranes
• Late or no prenatal care
 • Short cervical length
 • Sexually transmitted infections: gonorrhea, 
chlamydia, trichomoniasis
 • Bacterial vaginosis (50% increased risk)
 • Chorioamnionitis
 • Hydramnios
 • Gestational hypertension
 • Cervical insufficiency
 • Short interpregnancy interval (<1 year between 
births)
 • Placental problems, such as placenta previa 
and abruption placenta
 • Maternal anemia
 • Urinary tract infection
 • Domestic violence
 • Stress, acute and chronic

Patient Education about PTL
 Prevention
 Avoid traveling for long distances in cars, trains, planes, or buses. 
 Avoid lifting heavy objects, such as laundry, groceries, or a young child. 
 Avoid performing hard, physical work, such as yard work, moving furniture, or 
construction. 
 Mild to moderate levels of exercise are permitted such as walking daily.
 Achieve an appropriate prepregnancy weight. 
 Achieve adequate iron stores through balanced nutrition. 
 Wait at least 18 months between pregnancies. 
 Visit a dentist in early pregnancy to evaluate and treat any periodontal disease.  
 Curtail sexual activity until after 37 weeks if experiencing preterm labor 
symptoms.
 Consume a well-balanced nutritional diet to gain appropriate weight. 
 Avoid the use of substances such as marijuana, cocaine, and heroin.

PTL Education Signs and Symptoms
When to Call 
Notify your birth attendant if any occur: 
• Uterine contractions, cramping, or low 
back pain 
• Feeling of pelvic pressure or fullness 
• Increase in vaginal discharge 
• Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea 
• Leaking of fluid from vagina 
What to Do
Stop what you are doing and rest for 1 
hour. 
• Empty your bladder. 
• Lie down on your side. 
• Drink two to three glasses of water.

Nursing Management of PTL
See page 550 in text
 Early recognition and diagnosis is the most critical aspect
 Gestational age < 37 6/7 weeks
 Uterine activity (contractions)
 Progressive cervical change
• Bed rest with continuous Electronic Fetal Monitoring
•  Assess vitals
• Labs
• CBC, CMP, UA C&S
• Repeat electrolytes every 4 hours
• Maybe fetal fibronectin if suspect ROM
• Possible Medications:
• Betamethasone if 24 and 33 weeks
• Terbutaline limited to 48 hours
• Magnesium sulfate only as a neuroprotectant <32 weeks
(ACOG 2016)

PTL Care Management
 Early recognition and diagnosis
 Gestational age between 20 and 37 weeks
 Uterine activity (contractions)
 Progressive cervical change

Betamethasone for PTL (fetal lung maturity)
 Promotion of fetal lung maturity
 Betamethasone (Celestone): antenatal glucocorticoid
 National Institutes of Health (NIH) recommends for all women at risk for preterm
 Administered between 24 and 34 weeks gestation
 Optimal benefits occur within the first 24 hours
 Promotes fetal lung maturity by stimulating surfactant production; prevents or 
reduces risk of respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular hemorrhage in 
the preterm neonate less than 34 weeks’ gestation.
 Administer two 12mg doses intramuscularly 24 hours apart or four doses of 6mg 
12 hours apart
 Monitor for maternal infection or pulmonary edema.
 Assess maternal lung sounds and monitor for signs of infection.

Inevitable Birth 
 Management of inevitable preterm birth
 Labor progressed to 50% effaced with cervical dilation of 3-4 cm likely to lead 
to inevitable preterm birth
 Magnesium sulfate is given to reduce or prevent neonatal neurologic damage 
such as cerebral palsy before 32 weeks
 Malpresentation is common
 Labor may be very short
 1st stage progresses as normal but may not reach full 10cms
 2nd stage may be shorter 
 Increased risk for prolapsed cord (small fetal head) so AROM is not done
 Delayed cord clamping helps reduce need for neonatal transfusion
 Neonatal resuscitation
 Fetal and early neonatal loss

Premature Rupture of Membranes 
(PROM)
 Rupture of amniotic sac and leakage of amniotic fluid beginning at least 1 hour 
before onset of labor at any gestational age

Preterm Premature Rupture of 
Membranes (PPROM)
 Membranes rupture before 37 weeks of gestation
 Approximately 10% of all preterm births
 Infection is a major risk factor
 Pathologic weakening of the amniotic membranes
 Inflammation
 Stress from uterine contractions
 Other factors
 If labor does not begin within 24 hours and the fetus is 34 weeks or greater
  labor induced by IV administration of oxytocin so that the infant can be born before 
infection can occur
 IV antibiotics if viable

Care Management
 PROM
 Determine for each woman based on an estimate of risk
 Infection is the greatest risk
 Labor will likely be induced
 PPROM
 Managed conservatively to reach maturity 
 Usually hospitalized with ABX 
 May receive measures to prevent labor (terbutaline or mag)

Chorioamnionitis
 Bacterial infection of the amniotic membrane or cavity
 Prolonged ROM or PROM greatest risk factors
 Major cause of complications
 1% to 5% of term births
 25% of preterm births
 Clinical findings
 Maternal fever
 Fetal tachycardia
 Uterine tenderness
 Foul odor of amniotic fluid
 Patients with PROM or PPROM should get abx of they are >24 hours to delivery 
from ROM

Post-term Pregnancy, 
Labor, and Birth 
 A pregnancy that extends beyond the end of 42 weeks gestation
 Maternal risks
 Dysfunctional labor
 Perineal injury due to macrosomia
 Hemorrhage and infection
 Interventions more likely to be necessary
 Fatigue and psychologic reactions
 Fetal risks
 Abnormal fetal growth
 Macrosomia
 Increased risk for birth injuries
 Aging placenta=uteroplacental insufficiency 
 Oligohydramnios
 Care management
 Most physicians induce at 41 weeks gestation
 Others allow pregnancy to continue
 With assessment tests of fetal well-being normal
 Biophysical profile
 Nonstress test

Dysfunctional Labor (Dystocia) 
 Defined as long, difficult, or abnormal labor
 Ineffective uterine contractions (powers)
 Alterations and pelvic structure (passage)
 Fetal causes (passenger)
 Maternal position during labor and birth
 Psychologic response of the woman
 Increased risk for uterine dystocia includes:
 Overweight or short stature
 Advanced maternal age
 Infertility
 Uterine abnormalities
 Malpresentation and position of the fetus
 Cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
 Uterine overstimulation with oxytocin

Dysfunctional Labor (Cont.)
 Increased risk for dysfunctional labor includes:
 Maternal fatigue, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, and fear
 Inappropriate timing of analgesic or anesthetic administration (secondary 
powers)
 Abnormal uterine activity
 Hypertonic or primary dysfunctional labor
 Hypotonic or secondary uterine inertia
 Abnormal labor patterns
 Prolonged latent phase
 Protracted active phase dilation
 Secondary arrest
 Protracted descent
 Failure of descent

Dysfunctional Labor (Cont.)
 Precipitous labor
 Labor that lasts less than 3 hours
 Hypertonic uterine contractions
 Complications
 Placental abruption
 Uterine tachysystole
 Recent cocaine use
 Alterations in pelvic structure
 Pelvic dystocia
 Contractures of pelvic diameters that reduce capacity of bony pelvis, inlet, midpelvis, 
or outlet
 Soft tissue dystocia 
 Results from obstruction of birth passage by an anatomic abnormality other than 
bony pelvis

Episiotomy
 Incision in the perineum to enlarge the outlet
 Midline
 Most common
 Easily repaired
 Least painful
 Can extend to anal sphincter
 Mediolateral 
 Operative birth and possible posterior extension
 May have 3rd degree laceration with epis
 More difficult repair
 Greater blood loss
 More painful ?

Perineal Lacerations
 First degree
 Through skin and superficial structures
 Second degree
 Extends through muscles of perineal body
 Third degree
 Continues through anal sphincter muscle
 Fourth degree
 Involves anterior rectal wall
Lacerations

Forceps/Vacuum Extraction
 Forceps allow traction and rotation of fetal head
 Cervix must be dilated, presenting part low, bladder empty
 Vacuum extraction: a disc shaped cup allows suction to head head to 
facilitate delivery
 must show descent of fetal head to continue use, limit use to 3 pop-offs 
 Both: monitor fetal heart rate often
 Risk to mother: perineal lacerations
 Risk to Fetus: 
 Cephalohematoma
 Extensive caput (lasts several days)

Macrosomia
 Defined as > 4000 Grams
 Risks to Mom: 
 Cephalopelvic disproportion
 Dysfunctional labor
 Vaginal lacerations
 P/P hemorrhage
 Risks to Fetus: 
 Meconium aspiration
 Shoulder dystocia
 Fractured clavicle 
 Brachial plexus injury

Fetal Distress
Diagnosed by abnormality or change in the FHR or fetal movements
 Caused by inadequate oxygen supply to fetus
 Look for cause: 
 Position, vena-caval syndrome
 Cord compression or prolapse
 Medications: Oxytocin, Epidural or IV pain 
 Hypotension related to Epidural
 Try to correct cause:
 Reposition
 Give O2
 Decrease/medication
 Increase IV fluids
 May need emergency c/section

Intrauterine Fetal Death
 Accounts for 50% of perinatal mortality
 Many causes: PIH, IDDM, infection, genetic disorder, abruptio placenta
 Prolonged retention can lead to DIC -disseminated intravascular 
coagulation
 Nursing Care: provide privacy, do not leave alone, help with birth plans, 
encourage talk of grief, see, hold  and name baby, cultural, religious 
rituals, photo, memory box, follow-up counseling/support

Prolapsed Umbilical Cord
 Cord precedes the presenting part
 Risk: cord compression
 Risk to fetus: decreased oxygen flow to fetus, fetal 
distress
 Assessment: amniotic membrane status, as cord may 
prolapse when membranes rupture, check FHR as 
indicator of fetal distress
 If prolapsed
 Administer O2
 Apply pressure to fetal head with sterile gloved hand in 
vagina
 Hands and knees or Trendelenberg position
 (reverse effect of gravity) 
 Stat c/section

Obstetric Emergencies (Cont.) 
 Prolapsed umbilical cord
 When cord lies below presenting part of fetus
 Contributing factors include
 Long cord (longer than 100 cm) 
 Malpresentation (breech)
 Transverse lie
 Unengaged presenting part
 Care management
 27

Amniotomy
 AROM - Artificial rupture of membranes
 Done to induce or accelerate labor or to use scalp monitor- Cervix must 
be at least 2 cm dilated
 Risk: prolapsed cord
 Assessment:FHR before and after procedure, document amount and 
characteristics of fluid

Obesity
 Increasingly serious problem for pregnant women
 Likely to begin their pregnancy with pre-existing conditions
 Hypertension
 Diabetes
 Increased risk of postdate pregnancy and complications
 Nursing care has many challenges

Other Obstetric Terms
 Vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC)
 Indications for primary cesarean birth such as dystocia, breech presentation, or 
fetal distress often are nonrecurring
 May be a candidate to attempt vaginal birth 
 Trial of labor (TOL)
 Observation of a woman and her fetus for a specified length of time to assess 
safety of vaginal birth
 Often done with VBAC or suspected macrosomia or CPD

Meconium Aspiration Syndrome 
Meconium: thick tarry dark green/black substance contained in fetal bowels. 
Normally passed AFTER birth
 Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
 Indicates that the fetus has passed the first stool before birth
 Fetal distress during labor
 Fetal hypoxia
 Places the infant at risk for meconium aspiration syndrome
 May be admitted to NICU for observation or treatment
 Infant may need deep suctioning
 Intubation and/or ventilation
 Carefully monitor newborn respiratory effort
 Requires the team skilled in neonatal resuscitation
 Contact peds to come to delivery

Obstetric Emergency: Shoulder Dystocia
Shoulder dystocia
 Head is born, but anterior shoulder cannot pass under pubic arch
 Once head is born time to body should be less than 2 minutes.
 Nurse notes birth of head and begins timing
Shoulder dystocia is called if body is not born within 2 minutes
 Nurse calls out times to care team if shoulder dystocia occurs
 30 second to 1 minute intervals
 > 5 minutes = increased risk of fetal hypoxia and acidosis
 Newborn is more likely to experience birth injuries
 Brachial plexus injury
 Clavicular fracture
 Maternal complications
 Hemorrhage
 Rectal injuries
 Pubic bone fracture
 May need to get to OR for STAT c/s

Risk Factors for Shoulder Dystocia
 Longer first stage of labor
 Nulliparity, short maternal stature
 Macrosomia: Fetal birth weight over 8.8 lb (4000 gm)
 Previous shoulder dystocia
 Abnormal fetal presentation or position
 Fetal anomalies
 Maternal age over 35 years
 High caffeine intake
 Overweight/obese
 Gestational age over 41 weeks
 Chorioamnionitis
 Ineffective uterine contractions
 High fetal station at complete cervical dilation

Shoulder Dystocia Maneuvers
 Place patient knee-to-chest position McRoberts Position
 This changes the angle of the pelvis
 Apply Suprapubic Pressure NOT FUNDAL PRESSURE
 Locate fetal back-stand on that side
 Downward lateral pressure is applied to release the shoulder
 Woods Screw 
 Rotating the anterior shoulder to posterior

McRoberts Position
 38

Suprapubic Pressure
 Pressure to the anterior 
shoulder from the 
posterior direction
 Requires direction from 
the delivering physician
 In conjunction w/ 
McRoberts relieves 
50% of dystocias

Wood Screw
 Approach the posterior 
shoulder from the front 
of the fetus and rotate 
toward symphysis
 = 2 fingers behind 
anterior shoulder and 2 
fingers in front of 
posterior shoulder

 https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/video/how-to-deliv
er-during-shoulder-dystocia

Obstetric Emergency Uterine Rupture
 Very serious obstetric injury 
 Most frequent cause
 Scarred uterus as a result of 
previous cesarean births
 Signs and symptoms
 Abnormal FHR tracing
 Loss of fetal station
 Abdominal pain
 Abdominal rigidity=boardlike
 Shock
 Increased risk
 Multiple cesarean births
 No previous vaginal births
 Augmented or induced labor
 Multifetal gestation
 Macrosomia
 Infection
 Short interpregnancy interval
 42

Obstetric Emergency: Amniotic Fluid Embolism 
 Amniotic fluid embolism (anaphylactic 
syndrome of pregnancy)
 Amniotic fluid containing fetal cells 
enters maternal blood stream
 May be at placental implantation 
site
 Acute onset of hypotension, hypoxia, 
cardiovascular collapse, and 
coagulopathy
 Maternal mortality to 61% or higher
 Neonatal outcome is poor
